newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador seeks to save Galapagos from human trampling.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador seeks to save Galapagos from human trampling.

text.p: Ecuador is drawing up a law to protect the Galapagos Islands, one of the world's most unique ecosystems, from their worst enemy: man.
Damage to native species this year led UNESCO to threaten to drop the islands from its list of World Heritage Sites.

"This danger no longer exists. Action by the government has made this threat vanish. Now we are seeking consensus to draw up a new conservation law for the islands," Environment Minister Flor de Maria Valverde said in an interview.
The Galapagos, formed by solid volcanic lava, are famous for their unique flora and fauna, which bolstered 19th century naturalist Charles Darwin's theory of evolution.
Some measures to protect the islands are already in effect, such as limits on fishing within 40 miles (64 km) of the islands into the Pacific Ocean.
The government wants to restrict tourism and immigration to prevent further environmental damage.
Valverde said tourists would be allowed to stay a maximum of six months and researchers working on special projects would be made to leave when they finish their work.
Migration from the mainland has intensified over the past 10 years. Today 14,000 people live in the archipelago, many of whom have introduced new animals harming native species.
One of the unique species facing possible extinction is the "pepino de mar" or sea cucumber, a sea horse highly valued in Asian markets for its alleged aphrodisiac powers.
The minister acknowledged that some species face the risk of extinction, but said none have disappeared since the 1960s.

"We want to protect the islands and for that we need the support of international organisations and governments," she said. "We don't want the Galapagos to become another Hawaii, where for a long time now there has been nothing natural."

Ecuadoran and Asian trawlers, known in the ministry as "pirates," are blamed for harming sharks around the islands. Sharks found in fishing nets are killed for their fins then thrown back into the sea.
The proposed legislation is likely to spark controversy in Ecuador's Congress, even though the interests of tuna and sardine companies would be protected, a ministry source said.
President Fabian Alarcon is expected to send the proposal to Congress on September 1.
